title: 💥 Reaction Lab
description: Welcome to the Reaction Lab! You are a Grade 6 student stepping into the world of chemical reactions. Over 14 weeks, you will explore the difference between physical and chemical changes, discover the mysterious world of acids and bases, learn to measure pH, and witness spectacular reactions. From rusting iron to erupting volcanoes, handle acid spills, master neutralization, and present your discoveries at the Chemistry Fair. Can you become the Reaction Master?
subject: chemistry
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring chemical reactions, acids, and bases over a 14-week chemistry lab program.
Each week presents a lab challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and creativity.
Watch your dashboard — your Lab Stations (Acid Testing, Base Testing, Reaction Bench, pH Analysis, Safety Station) are interconnected.
NPCs like Dr. Litmus (teacher), Fizz (lab mascot), Anika, and Dev react to your decisions.
Random events like unexpected reactions and guest scientists will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Compliance high — acids and bases can be dangerous if mishandled!
learning_objectives: Distinguish between physical changes and chemical changes
Identify common acids and bases and their properties
Understand and use the pH scale to classify substances
Use indicators like litmus paper and universal indicator to test pH
Explain neutralization reactions between acids and bases
Recognize everyday chemical reactions like rusting and combustion
cultural_context: School chemistry laboratory, hands-on STEM learning, real-world chemistry in cooking, cleaning, and nature

behaviors.message: I am very concerned about safety! Acids can burn skin, bases can irritate eyes, and some reactions produce toxic gases. Goggles, gloves, and careful handling are NON-NEGOTIABLE in this lab.
The pH scale and reactions can be confusing at first. Come see me during lunch — I have a simple way of remembering acids and bases that will make everything click.
Outstanding work! Your understanding of acids, bases, and reactions is impressive, and your safety record is exemplary. I am nominating you for the Chemistry Star award!
I am amazed by your reaction experiments! You are thinking like a real chemist. I want to feature your volcano model at the Chemistry Fair!
Fizz fizz! Danger zone! I am detecting unsafe conditions. Remember: never smell chemicals directly, always add acid to water (not water to acid!), and keep the safety shower location in mind!
Bubble trouble! The equipment is corroding from acid exposure. Cracked beakers and stained test tubes give bad results. Time for a cleanup and replacement check!
Fizztastic! You are a Safety Superstar! Your careful handling of acids and bases is textbook perfect. I am awarding you the Golden Safety Badge!
All reactions under control! Your safety awareness and equipment care are looking great. Keep up the careful work, lab partner!
This is SO cool! Did you see the colors change when we added indicator? What if we make a pH rainbow for the Chemistry Fair? It would be amazing!
Hey, we are supposed to work together! Nobody asked for my ideas about the experiment. Can we please collaborate?
Whoa, you predicted the reaction outcome before it happened! And you were right! Your chemistry instincts are incredible.
Um, are you sure we should mix those without checking what they are first? Acids and bases can be really dangerous...
Excellent pH readings! I have been recording every test result in our data table. We have a complete pH profile of 15 household substances now!
We are not recording enough data. Without proper pH measurements, how can we classify these substances? Science needs numbers and evidence!
I plotted all our pH data on a number line. Look — most cleaning products are basic (pH 9-11), most foods are acidic (pH 2-5), and water is neutral (pH 7). Clear pattern!
Our team is working brilliantly. Everyone takes turns with the testing, recording, and cleanup. This is real scientific collaboration!

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the Reaction Lab
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the Reaction Lab! Dr. Litmus stands behind a bench covered with colorful liquids in test tubes, strips of litmus paper, a bottle of vinegar, and a box of baking soda. 'Chemistry is the science of CHANGE,' he says dramatically. He drops baking soda into vinegar — it fizzes and foams spectacularly! 'That is a chemical reaction. By the end of this course, you will understand WHY that happened.' How do you want to start?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your exploration of chemical reactions.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Learning safety and theory first means you can safely perform more exciting reactions later.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the difference between mixing (like stirring sugar into water) and a chemical reaction (like baking soda and vinegar)?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students entering a chemistry lab, teacher dropping baking soda into vinegar with dramatic fizzing, colorful test tubes, litmus paper strips, excited atmosphere

choices.label: A. A chemical change produces a new substance, while a physical change does not
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In a chemical change, the atoms rearrange to form entirely new substances with different properties. Burning wood produces ash and smoke — completely new materials. In a physical change, the substance stays the same — like cutting paper or melting ice. The paper is still paper, and the water is still water.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Cutting paper into pieces is a chemical change because the paper looks different
choices.feedback: 💡 Cutting paper is a physical change, not chemical! The paper still IS paper — it just has a different shape and size. No new substance was created. A chemical change would be burning the paper, which creates ash, smoke, and carbon dioxide — completely different substances you cannot turn back into paper.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. All changes that involve heat are chemical changes
choices.learning_concept: Heat in physical and chemical changes
choices.feedback: 💡 Not all heat-related changes are chemical! Melting ice uses heat but is a physical change — the water is still H2O. Boiling water uses heat but is also physical. However, cooking an egg uses heat and IS a chemical change (proteins change permanently). You must look at whether a NEW substance is formed, not just whether heat is involved.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Physical changes are permanent and chemical changes can always be reversed
choices.feedback: 💡 You have it backwards! Physical changes are usually reversible — you can melt ice and refreeze it. Chemical changes are usually irreversible — you cannot unburn wood or uncook an egg. The new substances formed in a chemical reaction are very difficult or impossible to turn back into the original materials.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus sets up six stations around the lab, each with a different demonstration: (1) melting ice, (2) tearing paper, (3) burning paper, (4) dissolving sugar, (5) rusting iron wool in vinegar, (6) mixing baking soda and vinegar. 'Three of these are PHYSICAL changes and three are CHEMICAL changes,' he says. 'Your job is to figure out which is which — and prove it!'
rounds.goal: Distinguish between physical and chemical changes and identify the signs of each.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: The key question is: Can you get the original substance back? Physical changes are reversible; chemical changes create entirely new substances.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is cooking an egg a physical or chemical change? Can you un-cook an egg? What does that tell you?
rounds.image_prompt: Six lab stations with different demonstrations — melting ice, tearing paper, burning paper with flame, dissolving sugar, rusting iron wool, baking soda and vinegar fizzing

choices.label: A. Signs of a chemical reaction include color change, gas bubbles, temperature change, or a new smell
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ There are four main signs that a chemical reaction has occurred: (1) Color change (iron turns orange when it rusts), (2) Gas production (bubbles or fizzing), (3) Temperature change (the mixture gets hot or cold), (4) Formation of a precipitate (a solid appears in a liquid). A new smell is also a clue!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. If a substance changes color, it is always a chemical change
choices.feedback: 💡 Color change is a clue, but not always proof of a chemical change! Mixing paint colors is a physical change — no new substance is formed. Dissolving a colored sweet in water changes the water's color physically. You need to check if a NEW substance was created, not just if the color looks different.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Chemical reactions only happen in laboratories, not in everyday life
choices.feedback: 💡 Chemical reactions happen around you every day! Cooking food, digesting your lunch, iron rusting, a banana turning brown, batteries powering your phone, and even your body breathing — all involve chemical reactions. Your body runs thousands of chemical reactions every second to keep you alive!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Bubbles forming in boiling water is a sign of a chemical reaction
choices.learning_concept: Bubbles in physical vs chemical changes
choices.feedback: 💡 Boiling water produces bubbles of water vapor, which is a physical change! The water is still H2O. However, bubbles from baking soda and vinegar IS a chemical reaction — the bubbles are CO2 gas, a NEW substance. The key question: are the bubbles from a state change (physical) or a new gas being produced (chemical)?

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus brings out bottles of vinegar, lemon juice, orange juice, cola, and dilute hydrochloric acid. 'These are all ACIDS,' he announces. 'Acids taste sour, react with metals, and turn blue litmus paper RED. But some are much stronger than others. Today we learn what makes something an acid — and how to handle them safely.' He hands out goggles and gloves to everyone.
rounds.goal: Identify common acids, understand their properties, and learn safe handling procedures.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk assessment: Not all acids are equally dangerous. Vinegar is a weak acid you eat daily; hydrochloric acid is strong and can burn. Learning to assess risk is a life skill.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Your stomach contains hydrochloric acid (pH 2). Why does it not burn a hole through you? How does your body protect itself?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench with bottles of vinegar, lemon juice, orange juice, cola, and labeled acid bottles, blue litmus paper turning red, students wearing goggles and gloves

choices.label: A. Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus paper red, and have a pH below 7
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Acids have three key properties: they taste sour (like lemon juice and vinegar), they turn blue litmus paper red, and they have a pH below 7. Common acids include citric acid (lemons), acetic acid (vinegar), and hydrochloric acid (in your stomach!). Never taste unknown chemicals in a lab — use indicators instead!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Acids taste bitter and feel slippery, like soap
choices.feedback: 💡 You are describing bases, not acids! Bases taste bitter and feel slippery or soapy. Acids taste sour — think of the sour taste of lemon juice or vinegar. An easy way to remember: Acids = sour (like Sour Patch candy), Bases = bitter and slippery (like soap).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Acids turn red litmus paper blue
choices.feedback: 💡 You have the litmus colors switched! Acids turn blue litmus paper RED. Bases turn red litmus paper BLUE. A helpful memory trick: 'Acids turn Blue litmus Red' — remember 'A-B-R' (Acid, Blue to Red). If red litmus stays red and blue litmus turns red, you have an acid.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. All acids are dangerous and should never be touched or consumed
choices.feedback: 💡 Not all acids are dangerous! You eat and drink weak acids every day. Citric acid is in oranges and lemons, acetic acid is in vinegar, and carbonic acid is in fizzy drinks. Your stomach uses hydrochloric acid to digest food! Strong acids like sulfuric acid ARE dangerous, but many acids are perfectly safe.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Not always playing it safe helps you grow as a decision-maker.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus now introduces the opposite of acids: BASES (also called alkalis when dissolved in water). He lines up soap solution, baking soda solution, toothpaste, bleach, and dilute sodium hydroxide. 'Bases taste bitter, feel slippery, and turn RED litmus paper BLUE — the opposite of acids!' he explains. 'Many cleaning products are bases because they dissolve grease. But strong bases can be just as dangerous as strong acids.'
rounds.goal: Identify common bases, understand their properties, and compare them with acids.
rounds.coaching_moment: Comparing and contrasting: Acids and bases are opposites in many ways. Understanding one helps you understand the other — a powerful learning strategy.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why are many cleaning products (soap, bleach, oven cleaner) bases rather than acids? What property of bases makes them good at cleaning?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench with bottles of soap solution, baking soda, toothpaste, bleach, and labeled base bottles, red litmus paper turning blue, students comparing with acid results

choices.label: A. Bases taste bitter, feel slippery, turn red litmus paper blue, and have a pH above 7
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Bases have a bitter taste, feel slippery (like soap), turn red litmus paper blue, and have a pH above 7. Common bases include baking soda, soap, toothpaste, and bleach. Bases are also called alkalis when they dissolve in water. Never taste chemicals in the lab — always use litmus paper or indicators!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Bases are only found in cleaning products and do not exist in nature
choices.feedback: 💡 Bases are found everywhere in nature! Baking soda is a natural mineral. Seawater is slightly basic. Many rocks and soils contain basic minerals like limestone (calcium carbonate). Your blood is slightly basic (pH 7.4). Egg whites, antacid tablets, and even some fruits contain natural bases.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Bases have a pH below 7 on the pH scale
choices.feedback: 💡 That is the pH range for acids! Bases have a pH ABOVE 7. The pH scale goes from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral (pure water), and above 7 is basic (alkaline). The higher the pH number, the stronger the base. Bleach has a pH around 13 — very basic!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Soap feels slippery because it is an acid that dissolves your skin oils
choices.feedback: 💡 Soap is a base, not an acid! Bases feel slippery because they react with the natural oils on your skin, creating a soapy layer. This slippery feeling is actually one of the key properties that helps you identify a base. Acids feel different — they can feel stinging or rough on skin.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus draws a number line from 0 to 14 on the board. 'This is the pH scale — the universal measure of how acidic or basic something is,' he explains. 'pH 0 is the strongest acid, pH 14 is the strongest base, and pH 7 is perfectly neutral — like pure water. Today you will measure the pH of everything!' He hands out universal indicator solution — a magic liquid that changes to a different color for every pH value.
rounds.goal: Master the pH scale and use universal indicator to classify substances by their exact pH.
rounds.coaching_moment: Precision over guessing: Litmus paper only tells you acid or base. Universal indicator tells you the EXACT pH. Better tools give better understanding.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is the pH scale from 0 to 14? What would happen if something had a pH below 0 or above 14?
rounds.image_prompt: Student adding universal indicator drops to test tubes of different substances, each turning a different color — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple — pH scale poster on wall

choices.label: A. The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is basic
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a substance is. pH 0–6 = acidic (lower number = stronger acid). pH 7 = neutral (pure water). pH 8–14 = basic (higher number = stronger base). Stomach acid is about pH 1 (very acidic), blood is pH 7.4 (slightly basic), and oven cleaner is about pH 14 (very basic).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. A substance with pH 1 is a weak acid and pH 6 is a strong acid
choices.feedback: 💡 You have the direction backwards! On the pH scale, LOWER numbers mean STRONGER acids. pH 1 is a very strong acid (like stomach acid), while pH 6 is a weak acid (like milk). Think of it as a countdown: the closer to 0, the more powerful the acid. pH 7 is neutral — right in the middle.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Pure water has a pH of 0 because it contains no acids or bases
choices.feedback: 💡 Pure water has a pH of 7, not 0! pH 7 is neutral — neither acidic nor basic. pH 0 would be an extremely strong acid! The scale puts neutral right in the middle. Pure water has an equal number of hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, which makes it perfectly balanced at pH 7.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. The pH scale only goes up to 7, with 1 being the strongest and 7 being the weakest
choices.feedback: 💡 The pH scale goes from 0 to 14! Values 0–6 are acidic, 7 is neutral, and 8–14 are basic. Without the basic side, you could not measure substances like soap (pH 10), baking soda (pH 9), or bleach (pH 13). The full scale lets scientists classify any substance as acidic, neutral, or basic.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus displays an impressive collection: litmus paper (red and blue), universal indicator (liquid and paper), phenolphthalein (turns pink in bases), methyl orange (turns yellow in bases), and your homemade red cabbage indicator. 'Each indicator has its own color range and its own strengths,' he says. 'A skilled chemist knows which indicator to use for which job. Today you become indicator experts!'
rounds.goal: Compare different indicators and understand when to use each one.
rounds.coaching_moment: Choosing the right tool: Just like using the right tool for a job, choosing the right indicator gives the best results. This is true in science and in life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do scientists need different indicators? Why is not one indicator good enough for everything?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench with five different indicator solutions in bottles, each producing different colors in acid and base solutions, color comparison chart visible

choices.label: A. An indicator is a substance that changes color depending on whether a solution is acidic or basic
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Indicators are like chemical color detectives! Litmus paper turns red in acid and blue in base. Universal indicator shows a rainbow of colors across the whole pH scale (red for strong acid, green for neutral, purple for strong base). Even red cabbage juice is a natural indicator — it turns pink in acid and green in base!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Litmus paper can tell you the exact pH number of any substance
choices.feedback: 💡 Litmus paper can only tell you if something is acidic (turns red) or basic (turns blue). It cannot give you an exact pH number! For that, you need universal indicator (which shows many colors for different pH values) or a pH meter. Litmus is like a simple yes/no test, while universal indicator gives detailed results.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Natural substances like turmeric and red cabbage cannot be used as indicators
choices.feedback: 💡 Many natural substances make excellent indicators! Red cabbage juice is one of the best — it turns red/pink in acids, purple in neutral solutions, and green/yellow in bases. Turmeric turns from yellow to red in bases. Beetroot juice, blueberries, and even rose petals can be used as pH indicators!

skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.

choices.label: D. Indicators work by chemically reacting with and destroying the substance being tested
choices.feedback: 💡 Indicators do not destroy the substance! You only add a tiny amount of indicator, and it simply changes color in response to the pH level. The substance being tested stays mostly unchanged. Indicators are like pH-sensitive dyes — they detect the acidity without significantly altering the solution.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! During an experiment, a bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid tips over and spills across a bench. The acid is spreading toward notebooks, equipment, and someone's bag. Dr. Litmus immediately shouts: 'Stay calm! Do not touch it! Step back from the bench!' The acid is dilute (not dangerously strong) but it will damage equipment and stain clothing. This is a real lab emergency — how do you respond?
rounds.goal: Handle the acid spill emergency safely and apply neutralization knowledge to clean it up.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience under pressure: A real emergency is the ultimate test. Staying calm, knowing the procedures, and acting methodically can prevent a small incident from becoming a big disaster.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does Dr. Litmus tell you to neutralize the acid spill with baking soda (a base) before cleaning with water? Why not just water alone?
rounds.image_prompt: Chemistry lab with acid spilling from a tipped bottle, students stepping back, teacher directing emergency response, goggles and gloves being put on, baking soda box visible

choices.label: A. In a chemical reaction, the starting substances are called reactants and the new substances are products
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In every chemical reaction, reactants are the substances you start with, and products are the new substances formed. For example: vinegar (reactant) + baking soda (reactant) → carbon dioxide gas + water + sodium acetate (products). The arrow means 'reacts to produce'. Reactants go in, products come out!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: B. Products are the substances you start with and reactants are what you end up with
choices.feedback: 💡 You have them switched! Reactants are what you START with (they react). Products are what you END with (they are produced). Think of it like a factory: raw materials (reactants) go in, and finished goods (products) come out. In baking soda + vinegar, those two are reactants; the fizzy gas (CO2) is a product.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. The total mass of products is always more than the mass of reactants
choices.feedback: 💡 The total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants! This is the Law of Conservation of Mass — atoms cannot be created or destroyed, only rearranged. If 10 grams of reactants go in, exactly 10 grams of products come out. Sometimes it seems like mass is lost, but that is because gas products escape into the air.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Neutralizing an acid spill with baking soda is a physical change, not a chemical reaction
choices.feedback: 💡 Neutralization is definitely a chemical reaction! When baking soda (a base) meets an acid, it produces new substances: water, a salt, and carbon dioxide gas (the fizzing you see). New substances are formed, which is the definition of a chemical change. This is why baking soda is great for cleaning up acid spills safely!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

rounds.situation: After last week's acid spill, Dr. Litmus dives deep into neutralization — the reaction between an acid and a base. 'When an acid meets a base, they cancel each other out and produce a SALT and WATER,' he says, writing: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. 'This is the most important reaction in chemistry — it keeps your blood alive, your stomach healthy, and your soil fertile!'
rounds.goal: Understand and perform neutralization reactions, and find the exact neutralization point.
rounds.coaching_moment: Balance: Neutralization is about finding the perfect balance between acid and base. In life too, the best solutions often come from finding balance between extremes.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you have an upset stomach (too much acid), why does taking an antacid tablet help? What chemical reaction is happening inside you?
rounds.image_prompt: Student carefully adding drops of base to acid in a beaker with universal indicator, watching the color change from red through green to blue, reaching exact neutralization point

choices.label: A. Neutralization is when an acid reacts with a base to produce a salt and water
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Neutralization is: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. The acid and base cancel each other out, producing a neutral (or near-neutral) solution. For example, hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride (table salt!) + water. Antacid tablets use this reaction — the base in the tablet neutralizes excess stomach acid!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Mixing any acid with any base always creates table salt (sodium chloride)
choices.feedback: 💡 Different acid-base combinations make different salts! Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide makes sodium chloride (table salt). But sulfuric acid + copper oxide makes copper sulfate (a blue salt). The type of salt depends on which acid and which base you use. 'Salt' in chemistry means any product of neutralization, not just table salt.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Neutralization reactions always produce a solution with pH exactly equal to 7
choices.feedback: 💡 Not always exactly 7! If you add the perfect amounts of a strong acid and a strong base, you get pH 7. But if you add too much acid or base, the solution will be slightly acidic or basic. Also, some salt solutions are naturally slightly acidic or basic. Getting exactly pH 7 requires careful measurement called titration.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. An antacid tablet works by adding more acid to your stomach
choices.feedback: 💡 Antacids contain bases, not acids! When you have heartburn from too much stomach acid, the base in the antacid tablet neutralizes the excess acid. For example, calcium carbonate (a base in many antacid brands) reacts with hydrochloric acid in your stomach to produce a harmless salt, water, and CO2.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus asks: 'Can you spot chemical reactions happening outside the lab?' He shows photos: a rusty bicycle, a sliced apple turning brown, fireworks exploding, bread rising in the oven, and a candle burning. 'Chemical reactions are happening EVERYWHERE, all the time. Your job today is to identify them, explain them, and find even more examples in your daily life.'
rounds.goal: Identify and explain chemical reactions that occur in everyday life.
rounds.coaching_moment: Connecting knowledge to life: When you can see chemistry happening in the kitchen, the garden, and on the road, you truly understand it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: A banana turning brown, a silver necklace turning black, and milk going sour are all chemical reactions. What is the new substance formed in each case?
rounds.image_prompt: Collage of everyday reactions: rusty bicycle chain, browning sliced apple, burning birthday candles, rising bread dough, fireworks in night sky

choices.label: A. Baking a cake involves chemical reactions — baking soda reacts with acid to produce CO2 gas, making it rise
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Baking is full of chemistry! Baking soda (base) reacts with buttermilk or lemon juice (acids) to produce carbon dioxide gas bubbles, which make the cake fluffy. The heat also causes chemical changes in proteins (eggs solidify) and sugars (caramelization creates the golden-brown color and delicious taste).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: B. A banana turning brown when peeled is a physical change because it is just changing color
choices.feedback: 💡 A banana turning brown is actually a chemical change called oxidation! The enzymes in the banana react with oxygen in the air, producing new brown-colored substances called melanins. You cannot reverse this browning. Squeezing lemon juice (an acid) slows this reaction — that is why cooks add lemon to cut fruit.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Dissolving sugar in tea is a chemical reaction because the sugar disappears
choices.feedback: 💡 Dissolving sugar is a physical change, not a chemical one! The sugar molecules spread between the water molecules but stay as sugar — no new substance is created. You can prove this by evaporating the water and getting your sugar crystals back. Disappearing does not always mean a chemical reaction occurred.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Digesting food in your stomach is a physical change because the food just gets smaller
choices.feedback: 💡 Digestion involves both physical AND chemical changes! Chewing is physical (breaking food into smaller pieces). But stomach acid and enzymes cause chemical reactions that break complex food molecules into simpler nutrients your body can absorb. Proteins become amino acids, starches become sugars — completely different substances!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus places three iron nails in different conditions: (1) dry air in a sealed tube, (2) water with no air (boiled, sealed), (3) water with air. 'We will check these in a few days,' he says. 'Rusting is one of the most important and costly chemical reactions in the world — it destroys cars, bridges, and buildings. Today we investigate what causes it and how to prevent it.'
rounds.goal: Investigate the conditions needed for rusting and learn prevention methods.
rounds.coaching_moment: Patience in science: Rusting takes time. Setting up an experiment today and checking results later teaches you that good science sometimes requires waiting.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Rusting needs BOTH water AND oxygen. Why does a nail in water alone (no air) not rust? Why does a nail in dry air alone not rust?
rounds.image_prompt: Three test tubes with iron nails — one in dry sealed tube, one in boiled sealed water, one in water with air showing rust forming — close-up of orange rust

choices.label: A. Rusting is a chemical reaction where iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Rusting is a specific type of oxidation. Iron + oxygen + water → iron oxide (rust). The orange-brown rust is a completely new substance with different properties from shiny iron. Both oxygen AND moisture are needed — iron does not rust in dry air or in water without oxygen. This is why painting iron protects it from rusting!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Rusting is a physical change because the iron just changes color to orange
choices.feedback: 💡 Rusting is definitely a chemical change! A new substance (iron oxide) is formed with completely different properties — rust is crumbly and weak, while iron is strong and shiny. You cannot turn rust back into iron by simply removing the color. The iron atoms have chemically bonded with oxygen atoms to create something new.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Iron only needs oxygen to rust — water is not needed
choices.feedback: 💡 Iron needs BOTH oxygen and water (moisture) to rust! If you place iron in dry air (oxygen but no water), it does not rust. If you place iron in boiled water with no air (water but no oxygen), it does not rust either. Only when both are present does rusting occur. Salt water speeds up rusting even more!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. All metals rust when exposed to air and water
choices.feedback: 💡 Rusting is specific to iron and iron alloys (like steel)! Other metals can corrode, but it is not called rusting. Gold does not corrode at all. Copper turns green (verdigris). Aluminium forms a thin protective oxide layer. Silver tarnishes black. Each metal reacts with air and water differently — or not at all!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Litmus lights a candle. 'Combustion is a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen that produces heat and light,' he explains. 'But what exactly is burning? What gas does it produce? Can things burn without oxygen?' He covers the candle with a glass jar — the flame slowly dies. 'No oxygen, no combustion. Today we investigate the chemistry of fire!'
rounds.goal: Understand combustion reactions, the fire triangle, and how fire can be controlled.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk assessment: Fire is both incredibly useful (cooking, heating, engines) and incredibly dangerous. Understanding the fire triangle gives you the power to START and STOP fires safely.
rounds.reflection_prompt: A fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat (the fire triangle). How does a fire extinguisher work? Which part of the triangle does it remove?
rounds.image_prompt: Candle burning inside a glass jar, flame getting smaller, student timing how long until it goes out, fire triangle diagram on whiteboard

choices.label: A. Combustion needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat — this is called the fire triangle
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The fire triangle shows that fire needs all three elements: fuel (something to burn, like wood), oxygen (from the air), and heat (to start the reaction). Remove any one side and the fire goes out! Fire extinguishers work by removing one element — water removes heat, a blanket removes oxygen, and removing fuel starves the fire.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.

choices.label: B. Fire only needs fuel and heat — oxygen is not involved in burning
choices.feedback: 💡 Oxygen is essential for burning! Combustion is a chemical reaction between fuel and oxygen. Without oxygen, fire cannot burn — this is why a candle goes out when you put a jar over it (the oxygen inside gets used up). In fact, combustion produces carbon dioxide and water. The oxygen from the air combines with carbon in the fuel.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. When wood burns, it is a physical change because the wood just gets smaller
choices.feedback: 💡 Burning is one of the most obvious chemical changes! Wood (the reactant) reacts with oxygen to produce ash, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and heat (the products). These are completely different substances from wood. You can never turn ash and smoke back into a log — that is how you know it is a chemical change.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Combustion reactions absorb heat from the surroundings and make things colder
choices.feedback: 💡 Combustion is an exothermic reaction, meaning it releases heat! That is why fire is hot and we use it for warmth and cooking. Reactions that absorb heat are called endothermic (like dissolving certain salts in water, which makes the water cold). Combustion releases stored chemical energy as heat and light.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! A student accidentally mixes two chemicals from the wrong shelves — the resulting reaction produces a thick, foul-smelling gas that fills the corner of the lab! It is not toxic at the concentration present, but it is extremely unpleasant and some students are coughing. Dr. Litmus pulls the fire alarm to evacuate the room and opens all windows. 'This is why we NEVER mix unknown chemicals!' he says sternly. The Chemistry Fair is two weeks away!
rounds.goal: Handle the unexpected reaction safely and learn about hazardous chemical mixing.
rounds.coaching_moment: Learning from mistakes: The most important safety lessons come from real incidents. This crisis will make you a safer, more careful chemist for life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it dangerous to mix cleaning products at home? What could happen if you mixed bleach with vinegar?
rounds.image_prompt: Chemistry lab being evacuated, windows open, yellow-green gas dispersing, students moving to corridor, teacher at emergency ventilation controls

choices.label: A. Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Exothermic reactions give out heat (the container feels warm or hot) — like burning, rusting, and neutralization. Endothermic reactions take in heat (the container feels cold) — like dissolving ammonium nitrate in water or photosynthesis. 'Exo' means out (heat exits), 'Endo' means in (heat enters).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: B. All chemical reactions release heat — there is no such thing as a reaction that absorbs heat
choices.feedback: 💡 Endothermic reactions are real and common! Instant cold packs used for sports injuries work by an endothermic reaction — when you squeeze the pack, ammonium nitrate dissolves in water and absorbs heat, making it feel cold. Photosynthesis in plants is also endothermic — plants absorb heat energy from sunlight.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. If a reaction container feels hot, the reaction must be endothermic
choices.feedback: 💡 You have the terms mixed up! If the container feels hot, heat is being released — that is exothermic (exo = out). If the container feels cold, heat is being absorbed — that is endothermic (endo = in). An easy trick: EXOthermic = heat EXITs. ENDOthermic = heat ENTERs.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Conservation of mass means that atoms are created during exothermic reactions to produce extra energy
choices.feedback: 💡 Atoms are never created or destroyed in chemical reactions! The Law of Conservation of Mass states that the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. The energy in exothermic reactions comes from breaking and forming chemical bonds — not from creating new atoms. The atoms just rearrange into different combinations.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: With the Chemistry Fair one week away, Dr. Litmus assigns the classic project: 'Build a volcano model that demonstrates a chemical reaction!' he says with a grin. 'But I do not want JUST a baking soda volcano. I want you to explain the CHEMISTRY — what reaction is happening, what gas is produced, how you can control the reaction, and how it relates to real volcanic eruptions.'
rounds.goal: Build a volcano model and use it to demonstrate and explain acid-base chemistry.
rounds.coaching_moment: Presentation skills: A great demonstration is not just spectacular — it teaches something. The best scientists can explain complex ideas in simple, exciting ways.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In the volcano model, vinegar (acid) reacts with baking soda (base). What are the products? Is this the same type of reaction as a real volcanic eruption?
rounds.image_prompt: Students building a papier-mache volcano model on a lab bench, one pouring vinegar into the crater, orange-red foam erupting, diagrams of the chemical equation visible

choices.label: A. The classic baking soda volcano demonstrates an acid-base reaction producing CO2 gas
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The baking soda volcano is a neutralization reaction! Vinegar (acetic acid) reacts with baking soda (sodium bicarbonate, a base) to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and sodium acetate. The CO2 gas creates the exciting fizzing and bubbling eruption. It demonstrates: acid + base → salt + water + gas.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

choices.label: B. The baking soda volcano erupts because the mixture gets extremely hot like a real volcano
choices.feedback: 💡 The baking soda volcano does not get hot like a real volcano! It erupts because the acid-base reaction rapidly produces CO2 gas. The gas bubbles build up pressure and push the liquid up and over the volcano model. Real volcanoes erupt from extreme heat and pressure underground — completely different mechanisms.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. In a chemical reaction, some atoms are destroyed and new ones are created
choices.feedback: 💡 Atoms are NEVER created or destroyed in a chemical reaction! This is the Law of Conservation of Mass, discovered by Antoine Lavoisier. All the atoms present in the reactants are still there in the products — just rearranged into different combinations. Count the atoms on both sides of a reaction equation and they always match.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Adding more baking soda to vinegar will eventually make the reaction go backwards
choices.feedback: 💡 Adding more baking soda does not reverse the reaction! The CO2 gas has already escaped into the air — you cannot put it back. If you add excess baking soda, it will just neutralize all the vinegar and then sit undissolved. The reaction stops when one reactant is used up. To get more eruption, you need more vinegar too.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Chemistry Fair day is here! The school hall is transformed into a chemistry exhibition. Parents, teachers, and students from other grades are visiting. Your bench displays your volcano model, pH rainbow, rust experiments, and indicator collection. Dr. Litmus gives a proud opening speech: 'These students now understand chemical reactions at a level that would impress university students. They are true chemists!' It is your moment to shine!
rounds.goal: Showcase your chemistry knowledge and make the Chemistry Fair a triumph for your team.
rounds.coaching_moment: Confidence: You have earned this moment through 13 weeks of learning, reacting, and growing. Trust your knowledge and share it with pride.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1 when Dr. Litmus dropped baking soda into vinegar, how much deeper is your understanding of that reaction now?
rounds.image_prompt: School chemistry fair with student booths, parents visiting, colorful pH rainbow displays, volcano model erupting, proud students in lab coats presenting, trophies visible

choices.label: A. Photosynthesis is an endothermic chemical reaction where plants use sunlight to make glucose from CO2 and water
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Photosynthesis is one of the most important chemical reactions on Earth! Plants absorb carbon dioxide and water, then use sunlight energy to convert them into glucose (food) and oxygen. It is endothermic because it absorbs energy from the sun. This reaction is why we have food to eat and oxygen to breathe!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

choices.label: B. Mixing salt and pepper together is a chemical reaction because it creates a new mixture
choices.feedback: 💡 Mixing salt and pepper is a physical change, not a chemical reaction! The salt is still salt and the pepper is still pepper — no new substance is formed. You could carefully separate them again (using water to dissolve the salt, or static electricity to attract the pepper). A mixture is not a chemical reaction.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Burning produces new substances, but the total mass of products is less than the reactants
choices.feedback: 💡 The total mass of products always equals the total mass of reactants! When wood burns, it seems to lose mass because the CO2 and water vapor products float away as invisible gases. If you could capture ALL the gases, the total mass would be the same. Lavoisier proved this by burning substances in sealed containers.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Chemical reactions can only be started by heating — no other method works
choices.feedback: 💡 There are many ways to start chemical reactions! Heat is one, but light (photosynthesis), electricity (electrolysis), mixing (vinegar + baking soda), catalysts (enzymes in your body), and even mechanical force (striking a match) can all trigger chemical reactions. Nature uses many different energy sources!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

glossary_terms.definition: A process where substances (reactants) are transformed into different substances (products). Signs include color change, gas production, temperature change, and formation of a precipitate.
A change in the form or appearance of a substance that does NOT create a new substance. Examples: melting ice, tearing paper, dissolving sugar. Usually reversible.
A substance with a pH below 7 that tastes sour, turns blue litmus red, and reacts with metals to produce hydrogen gas. Examples: vinegar, lemon juice, stomach acid.
A substance with a pH above 7 that tastes bitter, feels slippery, and turns red litmus blue. Examples: soap, baking soda, bleach. When dissolved in water, a base is called an alkali.
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or basic a substance is. pH 0-6 is acidic, pH 7 is neutral, pH 8-14 is basic. Lower numbers mean stronger acid.
A substance that changes color depending on whether it is in an acid or base. Litmus paper, universal indicator, and red cabbage juice are common indicators.
A reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water. The resulting solution has a pH closer to 7. Formula: Acid + Base → Salt + Water.
A chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen that produces heat and light. Also called burning. Products are usually carbon dioxide and water.
A chemical reaction where iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust). It is a slow oxidation reaction that requires both water AND oxygen.
The three things needed for fire: fuel, oxygen, and heat. Remove any one side and the fire goes out. This is the principle behind all fire extinguishers.
A mixture of indicators that changes to a different color for each pH value: red (pH 1) through green (pH 7) to purple (pH 14). Gives a precise pH reading.
A chemical reaction involving oxygen. Combustion (fast oxidation), rusting (slow oxidation), and apple browning (enzymatic oxidation) are all examples.

endings.title: Reaction Master
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Reaction Lab! Your understanding of acids, bases, and chemical reactions is extraordinary, your safety record is impeccable, and your Chemistry Fair volcano amazed the entire school. Dr. Litmus nominates you for the District Science Award, and the local newspaper features your project. You have proven that chemistry is the science of transformation — and you have transformed yourself into a true scientist!

endings.title: Skilled Young Chemist
endings.message: You have become a skilled young chemist with solid knowledge of reactions, acids, and bases! Your Chemistry Fair project demonstrates real competence in understanding and performing chemical reactions. Dr. Litmus is proud and says you are ready for the advanced chemistry module. Your future in science is bright!

endings.title: Lab Regular
endings.message: You completed the Reaction Lab program with mixed results. Some weeks were great and others were tough, but you stuck with it and learned the basics of chemical reactions, acids, and bases. Dr. Litmus says there is always next semester to improve, and the foundation you built will serve you well!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Reaction Lab was a tough journey for you. Acids, bases, and pH can be confusing, and the experiments did not always go as planned. But you did not give up. Dr. Litmus arranges extra sessions and says: 'The students who struggle the most often end up understanding the deepest.' Your story is not over!

endings.title: Lab Probation
endings.message: Due to repeated safety violations and low safety awareness, Dr. Litmus has placed you on Lab Probation. You can only observe experiments until you pass the safety certification. Working with acids, bases, and chemical reactions demands the highest level of care. Fizz the mascot has volunteered to tutor you. This setback is temporary — learn from it!

questions.explanation: The three common states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

questions.question: What happens to particles when a solid is heated?

choices.text: They vibrate faster and spread apart

questions.explanation: Heating gives particles more energy, making them vibrate faster and eventually change state.

questions.question: A chemical change is different from a physical change because:
questions.explanation: Chemical changes produce new substances with different properties.
